title: Model Selection and Optimization
intro: This is the second-heaviest domain on the exam. It spans four layers: how LLMs actually work (tokens, context windows, sampling, non-determinism, next-token generation, and prompting techniques from zero-shot to multi-shot), the general engineering fundamentals AI apps sit on (SDKs wrapping REST APIs, websockets, async patterns), how to choose among Claude's model tiers (Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) across quality/latency/cost, and how to manage tokens and cost with tracking, cost modeling, and prompt caching. Expect scenario questions where the wrong answers apply a real technique to the wrong problem — batch discounts to realtime chat, bigger models to rate limits, output trimming to input-dominated bills.

objectives.explanation:
An LLM generates text one token at a time: for each position it produces a probability distribution over possible next tokens and samples from it. Tokens are subword units — in English, roughly three-quarters of a word on average — so word counts only approximate token counts, and everything the model processes in a request (all input plus the generated output) must fit within its context window. Because generation is sampling, output is non-deterministic: the same prompt can yield different, equally valid completions. Temperature controls how adventurous that sampling is — low values concentrate on the highest-probability tokens (good for classification and extraction), higher values allow more variety (useful for creative tasks) — but even low temperature does not guarantee byte-identical output, so applications should validate meaning and structure rather than exact strings.

Prompting techniques form a spectrum by how many demonstrations you provide. Zero-shot gives instructions only; single-shot adds one worked example; multi-shot (few-shot) provides several input→output pairs. Examples are the most reliable way to communicate output format and edge-case handling — a model shown five tickets each answered with a bare category label will follow that pattern far more consistently than one merely told to 'respond with only the label'.

Models also expose options that trade speed against depth. Extended thinking lets the model reason at length before answering, improving performance on genuinely hard problems at the price of latency and additional token cost; adaptive thinking and effort levels let the model or developer scale that deliberation to the task; fast modes prioritize latency for simple work. The skill is matching the option to the task: routing an easy classification through heavy thinking wastes money, while denying a complex planning task any room to reason caps its quality.
objectives.whyItMatters: These mechanics explain most 'mysterious' LLM behavior engineers hit in the first months: flaky exact-match tests (sampling), requests rejected for length (context window), bills that don't track word counts (tokenization), and format drift that instructions alone can't fix (missing examples). Getting the mental model right prevents whole categories of misdiagnosis.

examples.title: Fixing a flaky integration test
examples.body: A developer's test calls Claude with a fixed prompt and asserts an exact output string; it passes locally, fails in CI, then passes again. Nothing is broken: sampling means run-to-run variation is expected behavior. The durable fix is to assert on what actually matters — parse the response, validate the JSON schema, check the extracted fields — and, where variance itself is the problem, lower temperature and add multi-shot examples to narrow the space of completions. The team also stops treating a single passing run as evidence a prompt change 'works', running each eval case multiple times instead.

examples.title: Choosing shots and thinking for two tasks
examples.body: The same team ships two features: tagging incoming tickets with one of eight labels, and drafting a root-cause analysis from an incident timeline. For tagging, they use a multi-shot prompt (five ticket→label pairs), low temperature, and no extended thinking — fast, cheap, consistent. For root-cause drafting they keep temperature moderate and enable extended thinking, because the task rewards deliberate multi-step reasoning and a few extra seconds is acceptable. One capability, two opposite configurations, each derived from the task's difficulty and tolerance for latency.

pitfalls: Asserting exact string equality on model output in tests — sampling makes output non-deterministic; validate structure and meaning instead.
Estimating tokens as words — tokens are subword units, so word counts understate token counts and break both cost estimates and context-window math.
Forgetting that generated output counts against the context window too — a request whose input barely fits leaves no room for the response.
Describing a desired format in ever-more-elaborate prose instead of showing multi-shot examples — demonstrations beat descriptions for format adherence.
Applying extended thinking indiscriminately — it improves hard reasoning tasks but adds latency and token cost that simple tasks never repay.

objectives.explanation:
Claude applications sit on ordinary web engineering, and the exam checks that foundation. The Claude API is a REST API spoken over HTTPS; the official Python and TypeScript SDKs are convenience wrappers around it. The SDK handles authentication headers, request/response typing, error classes, sensible default retries, and streaming-event parsing — but it does not change server-side behavior: rate limits, error codes, and token accounting are identical whether you use the SDK or hand-rolled HTTP. That distinction tells you where to fix a problem: serialization bugs and retry logic are client-side; 429s and 529s are server-side signals no client choice can bypass.

Transports should match traffic patterns. Plain request/response REST fits discrete calls. Server-sent events (SSE) — the mechanism behind API streaming — push a one-way stream from server to client, ideal for delivering tokens as they are generated. WebSockets provide a persistent, full-duplex channel, the right tool when the client must also push frequent events upstream (interruptions, live collaboration) over the same low-latency connection. Polling loops that approximate realtime are a smell: they add worst-case latency and waste requests.

High-volume integrations live or die on async hygiene. Concurrency (async/await, worker pools) keeps throughput up while requests are in flight, but must be bounded — unbounded fan-out turns a traffic spike into a self-inflicted outage. Every request needs an explicit timeout so hung connections fail fast instead of pinning workers. Transient failures (429, 5xx, 529) get retries with exponential backoff and jitter; immediate tight-loop retries amplify the very overload that caused the error. These are pre-LLM engineering fundamentals, but LLM workloads — long-running requests, streaming, bursty fan-out — punish their absence unusually hard.
objectives.whyItMatters: Most production incidents in Claude apps are not model failures — they are integration failures: retry storms deepening rate limits, hung requests starving worker pools, polling UIs that feel sluggish. Foundational engineering practice is what separates a demo that works from a service that survives its own traffic.

examples.title: Hardening a fan-out service
examples.body: A fintech aggregator fans out hundreds of concurrent summarization calls at market open and sees waves of 429s plus occasional requests hanging for minutes. The fix is three standard controls: a semaphore capping in-flight requests, an explicit per-request timeout so hangs fail fast, and retries with exponential backoff plus jitter so the retry wave doesn't re-synchronize. Notably, none of the fixes involve the model or the prompt — and removing the SDK, one engineer's proposal, would have deleted the retry and timeout machinery they needed while changing nothing about the server-side limits.

examples.title: Picking transports for a tutoring UI
examples.body: An ed-tech app needs the browser to render tokens as the model generates them and let students interrupt generation instantly. The server consumes the API's SSE stream; between browser and server the team chooses a WebSocket, because the client needs a genuine upstream channel for interrupt events, not just a downstream stream. An earlier prototype used 250ms polling and felt laggy while burning requests; a REST-call-per-token design discussed in review would have multiplied connection overhead thousands of times. Each transport matched to its leg of the pipeline keeps the app responsive.

pitfalls: Believing a different client (raw HTTP vs. SDK) changes rate limits — limits are enforced server-side; the client only changes how gracefully you handle them.
Retrying transient errors immediately in a tight loop — this amplifies overload; use exponential backoff with jitter and bound your concurrency.
Omitting client timeouts — one hung request per worker is all it takes to starve a service; hangs must fail fast and visibly.
Using polling where the pattern calls for SSE (one-way streaming) or WebSockets (bidirectional realtime) — polling adds latency and waste in both cases.
Unbounded async fan-out — launching every request at once turns bursts into self-inflicted rate-limit storms; cap in-flight requests.

objectives.explanation:
Claude ships in tiers with distinct design points. Opus is the most capable: deepest reasoning, best on complex multi-step and agentic work — and the most expensive with the highest latency. Sonnet balances strong capability with moderate cost and latency, making it the default for interactive products and most production workloads. Haiku is the fastest and cheapest, built for high-volume, latency-sensitive, simpler tasks — classification, routing, extraction, simple Q&A. Capability differences also extend to model options: newer, higher tiers support features like extended and adaptive thinking that budget tiers may not, which matters when a workload depends on them.

Selection is a quality/latency/cost triangle evaluated per workload, not per organization. The questions to ask: How hard is the task — does it need deep reasoning, or is it pattern application? What volume — at millions of requests, per-request cost differences compound enormously? What latency does the user experience demand? What is the cost of a wrong answer — is this an internal draft or a customer-facing action? A common production pattern is tier routing: a fast model handles the easy majority and triages the hard cases up to a stronger one, paying for capability only where it earns its cost.

Model choice is also a versioning decision. Behavior changes across model releases — formatting, tool-use habits, instruction interpretation — can break downstream parsers and workflows even as average quality improves. Production systems pin specific model versions, treat upgrades as releases (run the eval suite against the new version, compare, then promote), and never float on 'latest' in systems where a silent behavior change has a blast radius.
objectives.whyItMatters: Model choice is frequently the single largest cost and latency lever in a Claude application — often more impactful than any prompt change. Teams that default every workload to the biggest model overpay by multiples; teams that force hard reasoning onto the fastest tier ship quality failures. And unpinned model versions turn every upstream release into a potential production incident.

examples.title: Three workloads, three tiers
examples.body: A media-monitoring company assigns models deliberately: two million short articles a day get topic-tagged by Haiku, where speed and per-request cost dominate and the task is simple pattern matching; the analyst-facing research assistant runs on Sonnet, balancing nuanced drafting quality with interactive latency; the internal coding agent that plans multi-file refactors gets Opus, because that workload's failures are expensive and its volume is low. Inverting any assignment either multiplies cost pointlessly (Opus on tagging) or caps quality where it matters most (Haiku on refactoring).

examples.title: A model upgrade as a controlled release
examples.body: A legal-tech team pins their extraction pipeline to a specific model version. When a newer version releases, they do not switch traffic; they run their full eval suite against it first. Overall accuracy improves, but the new model wraps JSON in markdown fences in a small fraction of cases — enough to break their strict parser. They harden the parser, re-run the evals, then promote the new version behind a config change they can roll back. The same change deployed by floating on 'latest' would have been a mystery production incident instead of a line item in a release checklist.

pitfalls: Standardizing every workload on the top tier 'to be safe' — at volume, the premium multiplies costs for tasks a smaller model handles equally well.
Assuming prompt engineering can always substitute for capability — examples and instructions improve any tier, but they cannot manufacture reasoning depth on genuinely hard tasks.
Selecting on latency alone for interactive features — snappy wrong answers are still wrong; quality requirements bound which tiers are eligible at all.
Floating on the latest model version in production — behavior changes across releases can break parsers and workflows; pin versions and gate upgrades on eval runs.
Treating tier choice as permanent — workloads evolve, and a routing layer (fast tier for the easy majority, escalation for hard cases) usually beats a single static pick.

objectives.explanation:
Claude API cost is token math: input tokens plus output tokens, each priced per million at rates that vary by model tier (output tokens cost more than input). Managing cost starts with measurement: every API response includes usage data with exact input, output, and cache-related token counts. Logging that per request — tagged by feature, customer, or workflow — turns an opaque monthly bill into an attributable one, and gives you the cost model finance actually asks for: tokens per task times projected volume, per feature. Optimizing before measuring is the canonical mistake; you cannot pick the right lever without knowing which term dominates.

Prompt caching is the biggest lever for a very common shape: requests that re-send a large stable prefix — system prompt, policy documents, tool definitions — with only a small dynamic tail. You mark a cache breakpoint after the stable prefix; writing the cache costs slightly more than normal input, but subsequent reads within the cache's time-to-live are priced at a small fraction of the normal input rate. The discipline is structural: keep stable content first and byte-identical across requests, put dynamic content after the breakpoint, and use cache checkpoints deliberately in multi-turn or multi-stage flows. Anything that perturbs the prefix — a timestamp in the system prompt, reordered tool definitions — silently turns cache reads back into full-price writes.

The other levers each fit a workload shape. Batch processing trades latency (an asynchronous processing window) for a substantial discount — right for overnight and bulk jobs, wrong for a user mid-conversation. Right-sizing the model tier attacks the per-token rate itself. Trimming bloated prompts and capping unnecessary output attack token counts. The skill the exam tests is matching lever to shape: caching for repeated static input, batch for latency-tolerant volume, tier changes for over-provisioned capability, output limits for verbose responses.
objectives.whyItMatters: Token costs scale linearly with success — a feature that finds product-market fit can multiply the bill in weeks, and leadership's first question is always 'what is driving this?'. Teams with per-feature usage tracking answer in minutes and cut costs surgically (often 50-90% via caching and tier routing); teams without it guess, downgrade quality broadly, and still can't explain the bill.

examples.title: Caching a support assistant's stable prefix
examples.body: A support SaaS sends 30,000 tokens of system prompt, policy docs, and tool definitions on every request, followed by a short customer question; input tokens dominate the bill and traffic is steady. The team adds a cache breakpoint after the stable block. The first request each cache window pays the small write premium; every subsequent request reads the prefix at the deeply discounted cached rate, cutting effective input cost by an order of magnitude on the bulk of their tokens. The one prerequisite is byte-stability — they remove a per-request timestamp from the system prompt that had been silently invalidating the cache on every call.

examples.title: From surprise bill to cost model
examples.body: A healthtech product with four features gets a five-figure monthly bill and no idea why. The team adds middleware that logs each response's usage block — input, output, cache reads/writes — tagged with the feature that made the call. Within a week the data shows one feature, bulk report ingestion, drives most of the spend, and that it re-sends a large unchanging preamble per document. Two targeted fixes follow: prompt caching on the preamble and moving the latency-tolerant ingestion to batch processing. The other three features are left untouched — no broad quality downgrade — and next month's bill is both lower and predictable from the tokens-per-task model.

pitfalls: Optimizing cost before instrumenting usage — without per-request, per-feature token tracking you cannot tell which lever matters, and 'fixes' are guesses.
Breaking cache-prefix stability with timestamps, session IDs, or reordered content in the system prompt — every perturbation turns discounted cache reads back into full-price writes.
Applying batch processing to interactive traffic — the discount is paid for with an asynchronous processing window a waiting user cannot tolerate; batch fits overnight and bulk jobs.
Attacking the small term of the bill — trimming output tokens when input dominates (or vice versa) barely moves the total; find the dominant term first.
Estimating cost from word counts — the API returns exact token usage per response; word-based estimates mis-tokenize and hide the skew that drives real bills.
